source_basis: Primary article: larger spur circle increased pollinator use but decreased robber visitation; discussion attributes robber preference for small spur circles partly to avoiding pollinator-depleted flowers / energetic niche differentiation, not to a measured increase in bypass cost.
interpretation: Reverse sign is real but is not a clean relative-route-cost validation because bypass cost was not independently measured.

source_basis: Field bract-removal experiment: intact bracts enclose the spur/pedicel; removing bracts shifted the same Bombus from legitimate visits toward robbery while arrival frequency was unchanged.
interpretation: Direct bypass-protection boundary case: focal geometry hardens the robbing route.

source_basis: Primary population models treat corolla length as a mechanical bee-avoidance trait; longer corollas predicted lower robbing in the primary model, but the effect was model-sensitive and bypass cost was not measured separately.
interpretation: Consistent with a mechanical boundary case, but the relative costs of legitimate and bypass routes are not identified.

source_basis: Primary study identifies larger/more protective calyx geometry as a physical barrier to robber entry; severe robbery occurred in the shorter/narrower-calyx population.
L-morph robbed flowers had significantly deeper tubes, whereas the S-morph contrast was opposite and non-significant.
interpretation: No single route-cost sign can be assigned across morphs from the reported geometry contrast.

source_basis: Positive geometry-robbery correlations occurred in one of three populations and were not consistently recovered.
interpretation: Population heterogeneity prevents a single route-cost classification from the reported comparison.
